strength: Every number checks out against my data (31.9 vs 2.5 trials per 1,000 clicks, 1,316 trials, 412 vs 96), and the stop list, including merging dead posts, is exactly right.
mistake: The headline of 175 extra trials a month is a top-3 ceiling (it assumes /vs-google-analytics jumps to a 9% CTR), so it overstates what I should expect by day 90 even though it is labelled a ceiling.
to10: Give a realistic range for day 90 alongside the ceiling, and get the cookie-free page and the cookie banner post live in week 1 since they are the cheapest wins.

strength: An honest, checkable forecast of 42 to 125 trials with the working shown on every line, real dates, owners, keep and rollback rules, and a ready-to-paste title and meta for Monday.
mistake: It leaves decaying blog posts live and unconsolidated instead of redirecting them into converting pages, and it holds the cookie-free page until month 2.
to10: Add a small consolidation pass for dead posts and pull the 'website analytics without cookies' retitle into week 1.

strength: The seat math is tight and correct (733 vs 12 paid seats per 1,000 signups), security sits right before the 4-field demo form, and the A/B plan has a correct sample size and seat projection.
mistake: The hero uses our house line instead of Priya's 'email tennis' phrase, so the strongest customer-language hook is left only in a section headline.
to10: Put Priya's own words ('email tennis' or getting Monday back) into the hero and add one tactical answer to the 'calendars not kept current' objection beyond working hours.

strength: The hero speaks Priya's language ('No email tennis') with a round robin subhead that skips people who are off, and the deciding metric smartly requires a first booking within 7 days.
mistake: It asserts unsourced numbers ('three or four emails', 'your week gone'), places security three sections away from the demo form, and gives no sample size or projection for the test.
to10: Drop the invented email-count claim, move security next to the demo form, and add test sizing and the expected seat upside.

strength: The three numbers, the forecast miss, Customer A ($2.6M, 31 Jan) and a preview of the asks all sit in the first screen, and the runway math is correct for both September (52) and October (33/37).
mistake: It commits to a 27 November ship date and moving the role to New York as facts. Both are only noted as assumptions at the bottom, not flagged for the owner to confirm.
to10: Tie Customer A's exit to the expected NRR hit, and mark the ship date and the NY decision as to-confirm before sending.

strength: The burn-driver table makes the $2.2M rise easy to read at a glance, and the runway range of 33 to 37 months is correct.
mistake: The '$0.9M is roughly 9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop' math is shaky. It ignores revenue growth. 'Costing us more than it earns' is also an unsupported claim an investor could challenge.
to10: Drop the overreaching margin math, put Customer A ahead of the channel story, add forwardable intro blurbs, and show runway in the table.

strength: It aims at the right segment and trigger, opens on the pricing change and the rev rec rebuild, and keeps every step link-free. Each email has a low-friction one-word reply ask, and the 1,900-contact projection is correct (about 130 replies, 65 positive, 55 meetings).
mistake: It omits the basic compliance pieces (opt-out line, postal address) and does not exclude current customers or open deals.
to10: Add an opt-out footer and exclusions for customers and open deals, and move the 9-to-4 proof out of step 1 to keep the opener tighter.

strength: It is strong operationally: a this-week first move, a clean exclusion table, an opt-out footer, exclusions for customers and open deals, reply handling, and an A/B test plan.
mistake: Holding step 1 until the 12th to 15th can delay sends by weeks after a pricing flag and weaken the trigger that drove 7.9%. Asking for a 20-minute call from step 1 onward is heavier than a cold finance lead will want.
to10: Send within days of the flag and swap the early 20-minute asks for a one-word reply, keeping the operational extras.

strength: It names the Asia-Pacific overnight gap and leads with honest hard parts: the hours, a clear weekend rotation with a yearly count, and a local-time table. It also turns the application into the reply exercise, with hours math that checks out.
mistake: The application's centerpiece, 'a real ticket from the last 90 days', is never written out. It also puts 45% of the scorecard weight on interview rows, even though interview signals predicted little.
to10: Write the actual customer email for the application, shift more weight to writing (including handoff notes), and add a clear offer threshold.

strength: It follows the 0.62 signal all the way through. A ready-to-paste customer email sits in the form, writing to customers carries 50% weight and writing for teammates another 15%, there is a clear offer rule, and the review-hours math is correct (70 vs 160).
mistake: The 15% 'Conversation' line is close to the interview impression the data says barely predicts anything. The rotation and hours sit a few sections down rather than right under the salary.
to10: Make the interview score structured, behavior-based rows, and put hours plus the weekend rotation right next to the salary at the top.

strength: Every key number checks out against my data: 60% of Semrush losses from agencies, Lite at 70% of churners, 42% of AWT conversions from multi-site accounts. It names PPC parity as the wrong fight.
mistake: Move 5 (link-data content studies) is the generic 'do more content' advice I didn't want, and its success metric is loosely tied to the action.
to10: Swap move 5 for something tied to the agency pipeline or reporting habit, and add an exec summary that says what to start this month.

strength: An up-front summary lists lose, tie, win and 'not a Semrush problem', plus stop and don't-spend calls. A bold free-report-in-AWT move turns the 21,000 multi-site accounts into an agency reporting habit.
mistake: Move 1's report leads with organic traffic and rankings, not the leads agencies say they care about. 'Don't spend on backlink roadmap' risks starving our clearest lead.
to10: Have the report join client ad and analytics data to show leads, and soften the backlink advice to 'defend, don't over-invest'.

strength: The migration gates are very strong: 1,000 beta users on real setups with zero loss, a one-step undo, a top-200 extension test, engineers on daily support shifts during the freeze, and a staged update by default. This takes on the 58% ticket problem directly.
mistake: The calendar has no owners. The X thread and email still carry placeholders ([@author1], [Opens in __ ms], [Extension] by [author]). The 'ranked by users who stay' table is not sorted by its own users-kept column.
to10: Add an owner to each calendar row, fill or remove the placeholders so the copy can be pasted, and fix the ranking table to match its column (or call it ranked by retention rate).

strength: A dated calendar with an owner on every row that fits the team and the 1 December freeze. Sound math (17,080 retained in 2025; projected 6,980 to 9,240 from creators and authors). Measurable targets with plan-B triggers. Paste-ready X post and email that answer 'will my hotkeys work' and credit authors.
mistake: It doesn't add support capacity until plan B triggers. It keeps the staged 10% rollout as an optional 'bolder move' when it should be a default gate. The 'ranked by users who stay' table puts X (3,740) below authors (2,470).
to10: Make the staged update and an engineering support shift launch-week defaults, and label the ranking as retention rate or reorder it by users kept.

strength: It pairs a flat Agency plan for the leaky Essentials 8+ group with an honest fix to the hidden yearly option, backed by correct math and a candid point that yearly will not lift revenue inside two quarters.
mistake: Jargon and density (MRR, 'fence', per-account figures to the cent) push it past a grade 7–8 read, and hiding Agency from half of new visitors sits uneasily with our transparency stance.
to10: Plainer wording, and a test design that keeps the public pricing page the same for everyone (for example, test via invites) so nobody sees a hidden plan.

strength: Clear, on-brand Agency plan with exact, verifiable math, a named break-even point on Team move-downs, and go/stop rules that respect our principles.
mistake: It treats yearly billing as an aside offered only at the switch, instead of fixing the monthly-default pricing page and the missing in-app yearly offer for the whole base.
to10: Add a base-wide, honest yearly push (show yearly on the page, offer it in-app after 60 days) with its own numbers alongside the Agency plan.

strength: Fully on my data. It plans four narrator clips a week, half the slots on sleep and evening times, and maps all 24 posts by hook. The week 1 drafts turn my customers' own words ('replaying emails', 'quit by day three') into warm hooks.
mistake: It says no post needs review but sets no submission plan as a safety net, and later hooks like 'Awake at 2am' sit close to the insomnia line.
to10: Batch-submit weeks 2 to 4 for review on 16 November as insurance, and trim to stay clearly under 1,200 words.

strength: Clean, correct plan with the right mix and stop list, plus a smart review step: submit weeks 2 to 4 in one batch on 16 November so nothing gets stuck.
mistake: Weeks 2 to 4 get only broad angles, not post-level hooks, so the team still has to plan 18 posts.
to10: Add a 24-post hook grid and use the persona phrases more directly, including 'switch my brain off'.

strength: Every email pushes the two habits that predict retention. Each uses a real trigger with a skip rule, and email 5 targets whichever habit the user is still missing.
mistake: Email 5 is two branch snippets rather than full bodies, and the control group gets no emails at all, so it tests 'emails vs none' instead of 'new series vs old'.
to10: Write email 5 out fully per branch and run the holdout on the old series so the comparison shows the new series beats what we send today.

strength: The drop list is the sharpest of the two, tying projects/labels to the 'perfect on Sunday, gone by Wednesday' persona and planning the team invite's return in 2027, and the holdout runs against the old series.
mistake: It spends the fifth email on a Pro pitch instead of closing the gap on the second habit, and it sends the second-device email on a fixed day 3 even though a second-device trigger exists.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a 'the step that's left' email aimed at the missing habit, move Pro after day 30, and tighten to stay under 1,200 words.

strength: A trials-per-1,000-clicks and trials-per-page table makes the case plainly, and the ranked moves tie to the data with checkable arithmetic (for example +3,190 clicks and +100 trials on /vs-google-analytics).
mistake: The forecast assumes top-3 positions and 9% CTR on a broad head term, so the 175-trial ceiling looks inflated, and Month 1 packs three or more developer tasks into one day.
to10: Give a conservative range with a by-day-90 forecast, name the Month 3 comparison pages, keep the developer work to one day a month, and stay under the word limit.

strength: It opens with the decision and the bad news (clicks down 13%, blog worth about 56 trials), then gives realistic low-to-high trial ranges, dated weekly tasks, paste-ready title and meta, and keep/roll-back rules.
mistake: It says to leave decaying posts unchanged instead of consolidating or redirecting them, and it assumes /privacy-focused-web-analytics converts at the 3.6% home-group rate, which may be too generous.
to10: Add a redirect or merge step for dead blog posts, convert the cookie-free page at a more cautious rate, and trim to the 1,000-word cap.

strength: It states the segment case in two lines with correct seat math (about 733 paid seats per 1,000 recruiting signups against 12 for coaching). It also gives a rigorous test plan with sample size, a projection and a 4-field demo form.
mistake: The hero ('book interviews without the back and forth') uses brand-safe wording but not Priya's own 'email tennis'. The copy runs well past 1,000 words, and the security section mixes instructions to the team into the page copy.
to10: Build the hero around Priya's own phrase, cut the extras (test maths, bolder move) to fit 1,000 words, and keep the security section as pure page copy.

strength: The hero uses the customer's own phrase ('No email tennis') and names round robin that skips anyone off. It ties each proof point to the data, and its metric (qualified team starts with a first booking within 7 days) fits the segment.
mistake: Several slots are left as [bracketed] placeholders. It also mixes 'Get started' into team sections where the brand rule says 'Book a demo', and it adds unsupported details such as text reminders and 'three or four emails' per interview.
to10: Fill or remove the bracketed slots, use 'Book a demo' on every team section, drop the unsupported claims, and make the two hero variants test truly different ideas (pain versus outcome).

strength: The subject line and the opening admit the forecast miss and the margin drop. Customer A is the first item under 'what went wrong', each problem is paired with its fix, and the asks come with dates and forwardable blurbs.
mistake: It runs well past the 700-word cap. It also invents a 27 November ship date and states the New York base as already decided, though both are only flagged in the assumptions.
to10: Trim to 700 words by cutting the preview line and some table rows, give a ranged estimate of the compute saving from the 48-hour pause, and mark the dates and the New York decision as proposals.

strength: A clear three-number opening with a 33 to 37 month runway range, a burn breakdown table, and a candid section that ties idle AI-builder traffic to the margin drop and the low conversion.
mistake: It leads the bad news with the AI-builder channel and puts Customer A second. It also adds a confusing margin calculation (9 points against a 7-point drop), and the update runs over 700 words.
to10: Put Customer A first, drop the confusing margin arithmetic, merge the burn table into one line, cut to 700 words, and give each ask a short forwardable blurb.

strength: It targets the right segment and trigger, keeps every email link-free, and gives an honest expected reply rate that refuses to multiply the two gains.
mistake: The asks promise a one-page summary and 'three steps' that don't exist, there is no opt-out line, and it runs a little over the word limit.
to10: Add the opt-out and postal footer, make the asks things the team can actually deliver, trim to 900 words, and give a send-timing rule and a reply-handling plan.

strength: It is operationally complete: a first move for this week, a clear list and exclusion table, link-free emails, an opt-out and address footer, a send window tied to close week, and reply handling.
mistake: Step 1 asks for a 20-minute walkthrough straight away, which is a heavier first ask, and the 12th-to-15th send window delays some freshly flagged pricing changes.
to10: Soften the step 1 ask, reconcile the send window with the weekly flag timing, and tighten to the 900-word limit.

strength: Writing carries the heaviest weight (50%) on the scorecard, in line with the 0.62 correlation. The application is a ready-to-paste customer email prompt that replaces the resume and cover letter. The post puts $82,000, the overnight hours and the weekend rotation up front.
mistake: It adds a 100-word 'why this job?' question, which is cover-letter-like and adds reading load without any proven signal behind it. The interview signal (15%) is also thinly specified, with no set questions.
to10: Drop the 'why this job' question, add fixed interview questions, and tighten the whole piece to the 1,100-word cap.

strength: The post names the hard parts at the top. It includes a local-time table for APAC cities, and the hour estimates are correct. The 'ask 4+ scorers to be contacted next time' idea is original, and it gives structured interview questions.
mistake: 45% of the weight sits on interview rows, even though interview impression predicted performance at only 0.11. The application ticket is also left as a description ('a real ticket from the last 90 days') rather than written out, so the team still has homework.
to10: Write out the actual reply prompt, move more weight onto the written exercise, and cut to the 1,100-word limit.

strength: The numbers are accurate and show their working (agency 27 × 89% × 54% = 13.0 lost per 100 trials, Lite = 70% of churners, usage limits = 32% of all churn), and the answer says plainly that the biggest leak is our own Lite limits, not Semrush.
mistake: Move 5 (publish link-data studies) is generic content advice with a weak link to the evidence, and it takes a slot that a sharper idea could have used.
to10: Replace the content-study move with a bolder, data-backed idea, and put the Lite limit fix first as the fastest money while keeping the agency reporting bet.

strength: It ties the agency report, the 21,000 multi-site free accounts and the persona's own words into one coherent plan. It also gives a clear "do first / stop / don't spend" block and a fresh idea: a free report inside Webmaster Tools.
mistake: The Lite top-up is ranked second behind a larger product build, even though it is the cheaper, faster win. The Move 1 beta is also an ambitious first step for one month, and the piece runs close to the word limit.
to10: Rank the Lite limit fix first as the fastest money, and trim a little so it sits clearly under the word limit with a tighter risk note on the free-report idea.

strength: It ranks channels by retained users with correct math, which puts creators and authors first and Product Hunt last. It ties that to a dated calendar with named owners that respects the 1 December freeze, plus a six-point go/no-go gate built on the 58% migration-ticket problem.
mistake: Its support staffing for launch week is thinner than the problem deserves. It sets a 12-hour reply target but gives no extra hands, and the staged-rollout 'bolder move' is tacked on rather than built into the plan.
to10: Make the staged rollout and an old-settings undo part of the core gates, add engineers to a launch-week support rota, and trim the length to fit the 1,200-word cap.

strength: Its launch gates are the strongest idea in either plan: 1,000 real-setup beta users, a one-step restore of old settings, a staged rollout, and engineers on support shifts during the freeze. It also refuses to mention anything not in the build.
mistake: It is not ready to paste. The X posts and email are full of placeholders (speed number, author names, support address, first name). The calendar has no owners and is heavy for a team of one launch manager, one designer and one editor.
to10: Keep the strong gates, but fill in the copy, add owners to each date, fix the rollout dates (the plan says everyone by day 7, then lists a full rollout on 15 Dec), and cut the workload to what the team can do.

strength: One clean recommendation (a flat $79 Agency plan) with revenue math that checks out against the data: $249k for Essentials 8+, $24k lost each month, 29% of churned revenue. It also shows a negative downside case and a break-even point for Team move-downs.
mistake: Yearly billing is only a brief mention at the switch, not a lever of its own. The base case also assumes half of Essentials 8+ customers pay $15 more and switch, which looks optimistic.
to10: Make the yearly push (default or in-app offer) a costed part of the plan, and justify the 50% switch assumption or lower it.

strength: It reads the data closely: per-account math ($63.91, $120.85, $95.87), 374 customers and $23.9k lost each month, and a yearly-payer analysis that says plainly yearly won't help within two quarters. It adds a price-lock-for-yearly idea aimed at the 'creeping bill' fear.
mistake: It bundles Agency, a yearly display change and a 'bolder move' despite the ask for one recommendation. It is also dense with jargon (MRR, holdout) and runs over the length limit, and the mid case's 3.5% churn after upgrade is optimistic.
to10: Cut to one clear recommendation in plain grade 7-8 words and keep the yearly analysis to a short note, with more cautious churn assumptions.

strength: The data call is clean: half the posts on sleep, four narrator videos a week, evening slots, and a stop list. The projection is shown (12×450 + 8×100 + 4×95 ≈ 6,580) and the baseline of 10,900 installs from 76 posts is correct.
mistake: It sends all of weeks 2–4 for review even though nothing names a condition, and it never says which posts later in the plan would actually need review. Only the 6 week-1 drafts are shown, so the owner can't see what weeks 2–4 contain beyond four angle names.
to10: Give a post-by-post grid for all 24 slots with the review flag and submission date on each, and add the Headspace line 'Take a breath. You've got this.' to the drafts.

strength: It is the more complete and actionable plan. It has a 24-post grid, named owners with first-week deadlines, and drafts built on the customer's own hooks and the brand line. The success test is tied to the 90-day baseline, with high and low cases, shown working, and a clear 'it failed' line.
mistake: It declares no post needs review, but later grid titles like 'Awake at 2am' sit close to insomnia wording and are not flagged. The live-stream idea also adds risk and length to a plan that is already near the word cap.
to10: Flag the borderline later titles and say when to submit them, and trim the live-stream add-on to keep the plan within 1,200 words.

strength: Every email serves the two habits (recurring task and second device). Email 5 adapts to whichever habit is missing, the series stops once both are done, and the mobile-signup variant of email 3 comes with a fallback test.
mistake: The series runs over the 1,200-word limit and is dense in places. Email 5 is a branched email that is harder to build than a simple one, and the 10% control group gets no onboarding emails at all.
to10: Trim it to the word limit, and add a short typed example to the inactivity email and a per-email 'worked if' target for every email.

strength: Each email is clean and ready to paste: trigger, subject, preview, body, button, goal and a 'worked if' measure. The 'what to drop' section is persuasive and uses the data well, including a plan to bring the team invite back in 2027.
mistake: Email 5 spends a slot on a Pro upsell instead of reinforcing the missing habit, and email 3 goes out on a fixed day 3 rather than responding to what the user did. Users who haven't built either habit by day 14 get no further help.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a habit-gap email that adapts to the user, trim to the word limit, and make the inactivity email feel more distinct.

strength: It turns my October numbers into trials per 1,000 clicks and trials per page, ranks every move by extra trials and paid customers, and fills exactly 12 writer slots, including a GA4-migration page that tackles Maya's biggest fear.
mistake: Its headline gain of about 175 extra trials assumes /vs-google-analytics jumps to top 3 at the /vs-matomo CTR, which is optimistic for a far more competitive query, and it gives no month-by-month forecast.
to10: Give a realistic range of trials for each month, with dates and keep or roll-back rules, and do the quick retitle of the cookie pages in week 1.

strength: It reads like a real decision: bad news first (clicks down 13%, the lost blog clicks were worth only about 56 trials), a cautious 42 to 125 trial range that adds up correctly, dated tasks with owners, and clear keep, roll-back and scale rules.
mistake: It spends six of the 12 writer slots on refreshing existing vs pages and says to leave decaying posts untouched rather than merging or redirecting them into pages that convert.
to10: Swap two of the refresh slots for a GA4-migration page and a consolidation of the decaying blog posts, and retitle the cookie banner post in week 1 as a cheap early win.

strength: It shows the seat math clearly (733 paid seats per 1,000 signups vs 12 for coaching), uses our brand line for the hero, moves round robin, routing and security up, and gives a worked sample size so I know how long to run the test.
mistake: The hero uses our generic 'back and forth' line rather than Priya's own 'email tennis', and the PTO-skipping claim needs confirming against the product before it goes live.
to10: Put Priya's 'email tennis' wording in one of the heroes and add security proof right beside the demo form instead of one section above it.

strength: The hero uses the customer's own words ('No email tennis'), and the deciding metric, which requires a first booking within 7 days, is well argued as a guard against low-quality signups.
mistake: It mixes 'Get started' buttons into team-focused sections, which breaks our rule that teams get 'Book a demo'. It also adds a ninth open-source section that pads the page, and leaves several bracketed gaps I would have to fill.
to10: Use 'Book a demo' consistently, fold the open-source section into the security section, tighten the variant B headline, and say how many visitors and weeks the test needs.

strength: Puts the three numbers and the forecast miss first, and shows that $0.9M of extra compute on about $10.4M of monthly revenue is roughly 9 margin points, which fully explains the 7-point drop.
mistake: It never says when Customer A's $2.6M loss lands in ARR or what it does to NRR, and the 48-hour fix has no ship date.
to10: Give the fix a ship date and expected saving, say when Customer A's loss hits ARR and NRR, and summarize the asks in the first screen.

strength: A phone reader sees the bad news and all three dated asks on the first screen, and two asks come with ready-to-forward blurbs.
mistake: The runway row shows a 19-month drop (52 to 33 months) next to the table without noting that part of the burn rise was one-off, so it looks more alarming than the text explains.
to10: Add a note to the runway row about the one-off deposit, and say what Customer A's exit does to NRR.

strength: It goes past the pilot data with timing advice: start sends mid-month so step 4 lands before close week. It also covers opt-out footers, reply handling and an A/B test.
mistake: Step 1 asks for a 20-minute walkthrough, which is a heavier first ask than a cold, link-free email needs. The 'Last note from me' subject comes close to the closing-door urgency the brand avoids.
to10: Make the step 1 ask smaller, such as a one-line reply, and show the total meetings expected if all 1,900 contacts are eventually triggered.

strength: Very clear, honest reply-rate expectations. It says plainly that it does not multiply the segment and trigger effects, and gives per-100 and full-list projections that check out.
mistake: There is no opt-out line or postal address for consent rules. Step 2 drifts into a product pitch ('Chargebee is built so...'), and step 4 opens with 'I have not heard back', which is filler.
to10: Add opt-out and compliance footers, cut the product pitch in step 2, and time sends around the month-end close.

strength: The application swaps the resume for a real sample customer email that is already written, and the scorecard puts 50% of the weight on writing to customers, which is exactly what the 0.62 correlation supports.
mistake: The 100-word 'why this job?' answer adds reading time without any evidence that it predicts success, and the interview is scored as a vague 'Conversation' row with no set questions.
to10: Drop the 'why' question, replace 'Conversation' with specific interview questions tied to the job's hard parts, and add a sense check like 'about 8 or 9 weekends a year' so the rotation feels concrete.

strength: It opens with the honest hard parts (hours, 'about 8 or 9 weekends a year', working alone) and gives a local-hours table, which targets the early-leaver problem and the Asia-Pacific gap directly.
mistake: The application exercise is described as 'a real ticket from the last 90 days' but the email itself isn't written, so the team still has to choose and clean one up before posting.
to10: Include the actual anonymised customer email and a clear offer threshold on the final weighted score.

strength: Turns my raw tables into numbers I can check: 60% of Semrush losses are agencies, Lite usage limits drive 32% of all churn, and multi-site free accounts are 42% of free-to-paid conversions. Then it ties all five moves into one agency-reporting strategy, ending with a clever free Monday report inside Webmaster Tools.
mistake: The Lite usage-limit fix sits at #2 behind a report build that is still in beta, even though the data marks it as the fastest, cheapest money. The 'Here's the data' section is dense, which makes 'where we win' harder to scan.
to10: Lead with the Lite top-up as the quickest win, and give 'where we win' its own short, scannable section.

strength: The 'where we lose / where we don't / our biggest leak is not Semrush' structure is exactly what I asked for. It shows the working (27 × 89% × 54%) and adds the striking fact that only 37% of a Lite group survives 12 months.
mistake: Move 1's '19% gain' assumes every agency trial won back from Semrush converts to paid. That is an optimistic projection that could inflate the bet. It also stamps an invented 'November 2026' date on the data, and move 5 (link-data content) is closer to the generic 'do more content' advice I didn't want.
to10: Replace the content move with something tied to the agency or Lite signals, make the move 1 projection realistic, and drop the made-up date.

strength: A dated calendar with owners that fits the 1 December freeze, six clear go/no-go gates, and channels ranked by retained users with the math shown.
mistake: Extension authors are ranked #2 even though X kept more users (3,740 vs 2,470) and the reason isn't given; the 6,980–9,240 projection range is also muddled.
to10: Add engineering hours to the launch-week support rota and explain why authors rank above X despite X keeping more users.

strength: Strong migration gates: a 1,000-user real-setup beta, one-step undo, top-200 extension testing, and engineers freed by the freeze joining daily support shifts.
mistake: No owner per task, creators get the build only two weeks before launch, and the X thread and email are full of [placeholders], so the drafts aren't finished.
to10: Name an owner for every row, get creators the build earlier, and fill in the author credits and copy so the drafts are ready to paste.

strength: It goes straight at the Essentials 8+ leak (9.6% churn, about $24k lost a month) with one flat plan, correct base and downside math, and a clean test with go and stop thresholds.
mistake: It treats yearly billing as a side note at the point of switching, so it never fixes the page that defaults to monthly. That is the cheapest retention win in our data.
to10: Also make yearly visible by default and in-app for everyone, and size what that is worth inside the board's two-quarter window.

strength: It catches all three signals in our data: the 8+ churn leak (worth more than all 41,000 small shops combined), the hidden yearly option, and that the 12-month promise means only churn and uptake count in two quarters. It also gives low, mid and high cases and is honest about the near-zero low case.
mistake: The extra 'bolder move' and the 25-channel cap make the plan more tempting for Team customers to move down to. Adding those features drifts toward the menu I said I didn't want, and the mid-case churn of 3.5% looks optimistic.
to10: Drop the bolder-move section, justify why the cap is 25 channels rather than a tighter fence against Team, and tighten the prose to make it easier to scan.

strength: It moves the mix firmly to evening sleep posts and narrator clips, and the projections are worked correctly: 450 vs 95 installs per post, 3.4% projected save rate, 6,580 installs.
mistake: Weeks 2 to 4 get only a weekly angle each, yet it tells me to batch-submit them for review on 16 November, which leaves me guessing what I would be sending.
to10: Lay out all 24 posts by title and say which ones, if any, actually need review.

strength: A complete 24-post grid with owners, deadlines, wording that avoids any need for review, and high and low install cases with clear keep, rework or failed thresholds.
mistake: It drops text-on-screen video entirely with no test, and week 3's 'Awake at 2am' sits close enough to insomnia that it may need a review check it says nothing needs.
to10: Flag the borderline sleep titles for a quick review check and keep one text video as a control against the narrator clips.

strength: Every email serves one of the two habits that predict retention, and email 5 targets whichever habit each user is still missing, using only triggers the tool supports, with skip rules and platform branching.
mistake: The control group gets no onboarding emails at all, which risks losing users. Email 5 also needs two versions with different buttons, which adds build work.
to10: Compare the new series against a holdout on the old series, and give each email a numeric 'worked if' target the way the welcome email has one.

strength: The copy is clean and ready to paste. Each email has a clear 'worked if' number, the inactivity email is guilt-free, and the drop list links back to the customers' own words.
mistake: It spends the fifth email on Pro instead of pushing users to the habit they haven't formed yet. That weakens the focus on the 67% both-habits group, and the claim about what Pro reminders do needs checking.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a 'missing habit' email and send Pro after day 30 to active users.

strength: The numbers are right and trace to the data (31.9 vs 2.5 trials per 1,000 clicks, 1,316 trials, a ranked table with working shown), and it adds a GA4 'keep my old data' page that answers Maya's main fear.
mistake: The Rank 1 gain assumes the page reaches top 3 and a 9% CTR, a ceiling presented as a forecast. It also tells the writer to stop blog posts, then schedules a blog rewrite in Month 3.
to10: Give conservative and best-case ranges instead of ceilings, cut the loose Month 3 blog rewrite and the overloaded developer day, and include paste-ready titles and meta so the writer can start without any thinking.

strength: It is honest and conservative: bad news first (clicks down 13%, correctly summed), projections as low-to-high ranges that check out, keep and roll-back rules, and a Monday-to-Friday week 1 with a paste-ready title and meta in the brand's voice.
mistake: It counts refreshes of existing vs pages as writer slots, adds fewer new comparison pages than the demand supports, and says to leave decaying posts unchanged rather than consolidate them. Its 'refresh the 3 top vs pages' also sits awkwardly beside 'don't touch /vs-matomo'.
to10: Replace some vs-page refreshes with new comparison pages, add a plan to merge or redirect dead blog posts, and trim the length to fit the 1,000-word cap.

strength: The hero, "Let candidates book the right interviewer. No email tennis.", uses Priya's own phrase. The segment math is also right (1,540 of 2,717 seats, 0.73 seats per signup against 0.17 for sales demos).
mistake: It leaves several bracketed placeholders (security proof, tool logos, customer quote) and uses "Get started" on many sections of a team page, which breaks the "Book a demo" rule for teams.
to10: Remove the placeholders, use "Book a demo" consistently on the team page, add a sample-size plan for the test, and trim to 1,000 words.

strength: It is nearly paste-ready and rigorous: the seat math is right, "Book a demo" is used consistently for teams, and security sits near the demo form. It adds a test plan whose sample size (about 13,400 per arm) and seat projection both check out.
mistake: The hero uses the generic "back and forth" line rather than Priya's sharper "email tennis," and a few lines mix instructions into the copy ("Send this to your security team"). It also likely runs past the 1,000-word cap.
to10: Make Hero A hit harder with Priya's "email tennis" wording, separate the copy from the build notes, and cut to 1,000 words.

strength: The three numbers come first, then the bad news (missed forecast, Customer A, margin, stalled hire), and each item has a response. The direct-database growth of only 2.6% shows the growth is channel-driven.
mistake: The margin claim is muddled: it says the $0.9M is about 9 points of margin, 'more than the 7-point drop', which confuses the explanation. The email is also probably over 700 words and repeats itself with a burn table plus a full table.
to10: Cut it under 700 words with one table, state the margin link cleanly, put the asks near the top, and add forwardable blurbs for each ask.

strength: The asks are summarised in the first screen, and each names a profile and a date. Two come with short blurbs investors can forward. It uses the brand's own 'here's what went wrong and what we're doing about it' framing.
mistake: It commits to a 27 November ship date and a New York-based role as settled decisions, which are only stated as assumptions. It also never puts a number on how much of the 7-point margin drop the compute cost explains.
to10: Quantify the margin impact of the idle projects and the expected saving from the 48-hour pause, and give the New York decision a stated confidence or fallback.

strength: It picks the right segment and trigger, keeps step 1 link-free, uses the 9-to-4 proof as a plain sentence, and gives an honest expected reply rate with per-100 and full-list math.
mistake: It promises assets that don't exist (a one-page summary, the 'three steps that team took') and asserts product claims. Step 1 also pairs a question with a separate ask, and there is no opt-out line.
to10: Remove the invented deliverables, keep each email to one question and one clean ask, add the opt-out and sender footer, and trim the supporting text to fit the 900-word cap with room to spare.

strength: It leads with the decision and a first move for this week, gives clear load and exclude rules in tables, and adds send rules (opt-out, stop on reply, timing window) that make it launchable. It also includes an honest projection and a sensible bolder test.
mistake: Step 1 asks a cold reader for a 20-minute walkthrough, a heavier ask than the pilot's best performers suggest. Step 4's 'going from 9 to 4 is worth 20 minutes' edges toward implying a result.
to10: Use a softer, lower-friction ask in step 1, keep the proof framed as one company's result, and drop the 12th-to-15th send window that delays fresh triggers.

strength: It builds everything on the 0.62 writing signal: it drops experience, tool and degree requirements, gives writing 50% of the scorecard, and puts a ready-to-paste customer email into the application in place of the resume and letter.
mistake: It adds a 100-word 'why this job?' question, which brings back a mini cover letter and extra reading, and the whole piece probably runs slightly over the word limit.
to10: Drop the 'why this job' question, add a local-time table for more APAC cities, and trim to the word cap.

strength: The post opens with the hard parts (hours, weekend rotation, quiet hours) and a local-time table, which is candid, useful, and answers the leavers' complaint.
mistake: The reply exercise is left as a description ('a real ticket from the last 90 days') rather than written out, and 45% of the scorecard weight sits on interview rows even though interview impression correlated only 0.11.
to10: Write out the actual sample ticket, put the heaviest weight on the written reply, and trim to fit the 1,100-word limit.

strength: The numbers are traced and correct, including the 13.0 per 100 agency losses, Lite as 70% of churn, and the 12-month Lite survival of 37%. It also states plainly that the biggest leak is self-inflicted, not Semrush.
mistake: Move 5 (publish link-data studies) is generic content advice with a weak metric. Move 1's first step is 40 interviews, which is slower than starting a beta. The 'Data as of November 2026' date is invented.
to10: Replace the content-marketing move with a sharper, more original bet, and make Move 1's first step something shipped this month rather than interviews.

strength: A lose/tie/win/not-Semrush summary with explicit 'do first', 'stop' and 'don't spend' lines, then ranked moves that quote the personas' own words. Every move has an owner, a concrete first step this month and a metric.
mistake: Some metrics are stretched: a Lite top-up is expected to lift in-house trial-to-paid, and the enterprise vendor-consolidation line is loosely tied to Semrush. The free-report move risks cannibalising paid plans.
to10: Tie every success metric directly to its move, and add a clearer revenue-risk test for the free Webmaster Tools report.

strength: Eight clear go/no-go gates (1,000-user migration beta, undo, support with engineers on shifts, staged rollout) tied to the 58% migration-ticket problem, plus a dated plan with a retention-ranked channel table.
mistake: The X thread and email are full of placeholders ([__ ms on a __ Mac], [@author1], [first name], [support address]). The plan also runs too long and asks for extra builds (an undo feature, a 1,000-user beta) that are hard to fit before the freeze.
to10: Cut the length and the placeholders, drop or justify the undo feature given the freeze, and deliver a launch-day post and email that can be pasted as written.

strength: It opens with a clear decision (community first, no launch unless carry-over is proven) and works backward from the 1 December freeze: author build on 17 Nov, bug triage by 27 Nov, an owner on every dated row, plus measures, plan B and a staged-rollout option.
mistake: It runs over the 1,200-word limit and makes no use of engineering to help support during launch week, so the 12-hour reply target rests on a projection.
to10: Trim to the word limit and add a concrete launch-week support staffing plan (for example, engineers on shifts) behind the reply-time target.

strength: One clear Agency plan aimed at the Essentials 8+ leak, with revenue math that checks out ($249k group, $24k lost a month, $2.21M total) and a break-even point: it loses money if more than about 1 in 3 Team 8+ customers move down.
mistake: Yearly billing, the cheap quick win in the data, is mentioned only as an offer at the switch. The default-to-monthly page and the missing in-app yearly offer are never fixed.
to10: Add the no-price-change yearly fix for everyone, and show the Agency gain as churn reduction against cash timing in the first two quarters.

strength: Pairs the Agency plan with a no-cost fix to the yearly toggle. It states the bad news up front (low case near zero, nothing from repricing inside the board's window), gives low, mid and high cases, and sets stop rules including MRR per account against a holdout, with dates and a this-week step.
mistake: The yearly-versus-monthly math is confusing and hedged, and the added 'bolder move' (lock the price for yearly payers) drifts from the owner's request for one recommendation, not a menu.
to10: Drop or shrink the bolder move and the yearly side calculation, and tighten the prose so the page is as easy to read as the decision itself.

strength: It builds the whole plan on the data: sleep-led, narrator clips as the core format, evening slots. It maps all 24 posts and writes six drafts in the warm voice, using the customer's own hooks and ending each on one small thing to do.
mistake: It probably runs over the 1,200-word cap. The live-stream 'bolder move' is also an untested extra, and 'Awake at 2am' in week 3 may trigger review that the plan doesn't flag.
to10: Trim to the word limit, drop the live-stream tangent, and flag which later-week titles (like 'Awake at 2am') would need review and when to submit them.

strength: It is concise and clear. It leads with sleep, narrator video and evening posting, and gives a sensible success test: 5,000 installs and a 4% save rate on narrator videos, with the caveat that the 5.9% came from only 5 posts.
mistake: It sends all of weeks 2 to 4 for review, which the plan doesn't need, and then says approved posts go live from Tuesday 24 November while still scheduling a Monday 23 November post. It also gives only weekly themes for weeks 2 to 4, not post-level ideas.
to10: Give a post-level calendar for all four weeks, fix the Monday 23 November conflict with the review timing, and cut stress at work and kindness carousels further in favour of sleep and narrator clips.

strength: The whole series is built on the two retention habits (recurring task and second device). It skips emails already done, branches on signup platform, and ends with a day-8 email that points each user to the habit they're missing.
mistake: Success measures are mostly series-level rather than a clear 'worked if' per email. The day-8 email also relies on branching by past behavior, which the tool may not support, and the control group gets no onboarding emails at all.
to10: Give each email its own 'worked if' line, make the day-8 branching explicitly rely only on the allowed triggers, and trim to the 1,200-word limit.

strength: Every email has a trigger, a typed example in quotes, a button, a goal and a baseline-linked 'worked if'. The drop list is detailed with numbers and a sensible plan to bring the team invite back in 2027.
mistake: The fifth email is a Pro upsell with a Pro-feature claim that wasn't in the brief. It spends the final slot on selling instead of closing the gap on the missing habit, so the series never targets the 67% both-habits group.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a 'the step that's left' email aimed at the missing habit, and cut the length to the 1,200-word limit.

strength: Every forecast traces to my data: the 18–46 trials on the GA page come from a 4.5–6% CTR on 58,000 impressions converting at 3.2%, and the 42–125 total sums exactly from the rows. It is dated (16 Nov is a Monday), and it gives keep, roll-back and scale rules.
mistake: It says to leave decaying blog posts live and unchanged instead of consolidating or redirecting them into the pages that convert. The move-4 cell ('0 on page two, 29 at 3.5% CTR') is too cryptic to scan.
to10: Add a merge-and-redirect step for dead blog posts in a developer day, and rewrite the move-4 projection in plain words.

strength: The trials-per-1,000-clicks table makes the case at a glance (31.9 for comparison pages, 2.5 for blog). It adds a GA4 migration page aimed at Maya's real blocker, and it plans to merge and redirect dead posts.
mistake: The headline of 175 extra trials rests on /vs-google-analytics jumping from position 4.2 into the top 3, which is a ceiling and not a forecast. It also hands an audit to a 'strategist' I don't have on the team.
to10: Give a realistic month-by-month trial range rather than a ceiling, and write the actual new title and meta for Monday instead of asking the writer to come up with them.

strength: The segment math is right and sharp: 0.73 paid seats per recruiting signup against 0.17 for team sales demos. The page leads with email tennis and moves round robin and routing up with the real 88% and 74% figures.
mistake: Security sits in section 6 of 9, three sections above the demo form. It does not remove Priya's main blocker at the moment she would click.
to10: Put security proof directly beside the demo form, cut the bracket placeholders to one clear caveat, and add a sample size so the two-week minimum means something.

strength: The flow matches how Priya buys. Security sits right before a 4-field demo form, plus a 'send to your security team' idea in the confirmation email. The sample size and seat projection check out (about 13,400 per arm; 150 to 460 seats).
mistake: The sample size uses the 3.1% homepage signup rate as the baseline for a narrower metric (demos plus recruiting signups only), so the real test likely needs more visitors and runs longer than stated.
to10: Base the power calculation on the current recruiting-visitor start rate, and keep each section to one action instead of a button plus a 'Get started' text link.

strength: Sharp, checked analysis: it splits out the AI-builder and direct database counts (direct up only 2.6%), sizes the $0.9M compute rise against about $10.4M of monthly revenue, gets runway right at 33 to 37 months, and breaks down the $2.2M burn rise in a clean table.
mistake: Customer A's $2.6M loss sits second under 'What went wrong', after a long AI-builder paragraph, and is left out of the subject and headline numbers, so a phone reader may not see it on the first screen; the hit to NRR or February ARR is never mentioned.
to10: Put Customer A and the asks in the subject or opening lines, say when the loss shows up in ARR and NRR, and give the 48-hour pause a ship date.

strength: Built for a partner reading on a phone: the subject names the miss and the margin drop, the preview names the lost customer, the three asks with dates sit above the fold, Customer A leads the bad news with when it hits ARR, and the asks include ready-to-forward blurbs.
mistake: It states decisions as done ('the role is now based in New York', 'ships by 27 November') that the founders have not confirmed, and the 52-to-33-month runway row looks alarming because the one-off deposit is only explained elsewhere.
to10: Mark the New York base and ship date as proposals to confirm, add a note on the NRR impact of Customer A, and footnote the runway row with the 37-month figure that excludes the deposit.

strength: It aims at exactly the right segment and trigger, keeps every step link-free with low-friction one-word reply asks, and projects 7% replies and about 55 meetings from the 1,900 with sound arithmetic.
mistake: No opt-out line or postal address in the emails, and no exclusion of current customers, open deals or past opt-outs, so it isn't safe to send as written.
to10: Add the opt-out footer and suppression rules, plus a reply-handling plan and a subject-line test from day one.

strength: It gives a clear first move this week, the right segment and trigger, an opt-out footer, suppression of customers, open deals and opt-outs, reply handling and a subject-line A/B test, so it is closer to a launchable playbook.
mistake: Asking for a 20-minute call in step 1 and a joint call with engineering in step 2 is heavier than a cold first touch needs. The 12th-to-15th send window could also let the 60-day pricing trigger go stale.
to10: Swap the early meeting asks for low-commitment replies, let flagged contacts start within days rather than waiting for a calendar window, and show total projected meetings from the 1,900.

strength: The application really is the 0.62 signal: a ready-to-paste locked-out HEY customer email with a 200-word cap replaces the resume. Writing is weighted 50% and the review maths checks out (160h ÷ 2,100 = 4.6 min; 2,100 × 2 min = 70h, 90h saved).
mistake: The weekend rotation gets its own section, but it sits below hours and pay instead of leading the 'hard parts' list. The 2-minutes-per-reply estimate is an optimistic single number with no range.
to10: Lead the hard parts with the weekend rotation, give local times for Tokyo and Sydney, and show a review-hours range with the second-pass cost built in.

strength: The post opens with the overnight gap and $82,000, then puts hours and the one-in-six weekend (about 8 or 9 a year) at the top of the hard parts. The local-time table is correct, including Sydney daylight saving, and the costed review plan holds up (94 to 129h, 6 to 9h per reviewer per week).
mistake: It says to use 'a real ticket' but doesn't supply one, so the application isn't paste-ready. It gives 45% of the weight to interview rows and has no offer threshold.
to10: Include the actual customer email and an offer rule such as 4.0+ with no row below 3, and keep the interview weight lower given its 0.11 correlation.

strength: Every key number checks out: 13.0 of 21.6 Semrush losses per 100 trials are agency (60%), Lite is 70% of churn, and multi-site AWT accounts are 42% of free conversions. It ties moves 1, 3 and 5 into one agency reporting bet and says not to chase PPC parity.
mistake: The Lite usage-limit fix, the fastest and cheapest money, sits at #2 behind a product build with no reason given, and the ranking is by customers affected rather than effort.
to10: Put the Lite top-up first as the quick win, or explain why the reporting beta outranks it, and add rough effort or cost to each move.

strength: A very clear 'where we lose / where we don't / our biggest leak isn't Semrush' structure with correct working, including the useful Lite retention point (37% left after 12 months) and an explicit 'what we should not do' list.
mistake: Move 5, link-data content studies, is the generic 'do more content' advice the owner dislikes, and move 1's first step is research interviews rather than something that ships. The 'November 2026' data date is invented.
to10: Replace move 5 with a move tied to the agency pipeline, such as a free report in AWT, and give move 1 a first step that ships a beta this month.

strength: A dated calendar with named owners that fits our small team and the 1 December freeze. Authors get the build on 17 November so their bugs land before the freeze. Retention math is correct throughout (4,510 / 2,470 / 3,740 / 2,940 / 3,420; 17,080 total), and the 9-creator projection is right.
mistake: The launch X post credits '1,500 extension authors' generically instead of naming the authors whose extensions appear in the clip. The creator brief is only invite-and-embargo, with no angle per persona.
to10: Name specific authors in the X post and email, and give creators a two-angle brief (upgrade for power users, first-day setup for newcomers).

strength: Sharp safeguards. A one-step settings undo, a 1,000-user real-setup migration beta, any speed claim held until it is measured, and engineers freed by the freeze joining support shifts. Retention math is also right (about 750 per video, about 6,750 for 9 creators).
mistake: The calendar lists audiences, not owners, so I can't see who does what. Creators get the build only on 24 November and clips are cut from 1 December, which is tight. The X thread and email are full of placeholders ([ms], [@author], [first name], [support address]).
to10: Add an owner to every dated task, get the build to creators a week earlier, and fill the placeholders so the copy can ship.

strength: It finds both levers: a flat Agency plan for the 9.6%-churn Essentials 8+ group, and showing yearly billing to everyone now. The math checks: $63.91 per account, $23,900 MRR lost each month, $2.21M total, and the $58.09 vs $60 yearly working is correct.
mistake: The yearly section is dense with numbers like $32.59 and 3.4% that a grade 7-8 reader will struggle with. It also never estimates how many more people a visible yearly option would convert.
to10: Simplify the yearly paragraph and add an estimate of the retention gain from moving yearly uptake from 19% to a target share, with its own stop rule.

strength: A clear Agency plan with traceable math: $249k Essentials 8+ revenue, +$2.7k on day of switch and +$23.0k at month 6. It has an honest downside case, the 1-in-3 Team move-down break-even, and a warm customer email that shows each person's own bill.
mistake: It treats yearly billing only as an offer at the moment of switching. That misses the cheap fix of defaulting or re-offering yearly to everyone. It also quotes 11 channels on Team at $121, which is the 10.4-channel figure (the real cost is about $128), and it presents the $276k annualized run rate as if it were earned within the board's two quarters.
to10: Add a store-wide yearly-visibility change with its retention math, and separate run-rate from revenue actually earned inside the two quarters.

strength: It plans all 24 posts by title inside the 4-clip, 6-post limits, sets evening times and sleep-heavy themes, and gives a dated first move, a projection with the working shown, and decision rules for 30 November and 14 December.
mistake: Some drafts tell rather than invite ('Grab a scrap of paper', 'Lower the volume and press play'), and the install projection is a couple off (6,582 and 4,782 should be 6,580 and 4,780).
to10: Recast the instructive lines as invitations, and flag that the week-3 'Awake at 2am' post must be worded so it doesn't imply insomnia and trigger review.

strength: The drafts are warm and invitational ('Want to try?'), use the customers' own phrases, end with one small action, and are backed by correct per-theme install, save and share baselines plus a sensible check on whether the 5.9% narrator result holds at scale.
mistake: It sends all of weeks 2 to 4 into review on 16 November, then says posts can go live from Tuesday 24 November, which strands the Monday 23 November post that the same plan schedules.
to10: Send only posts that name a condition for review, so the Monday 23 November slot isn't blocked, and give per-post topics for weeks 2 to 4 rather than just weekly angles.

strength: Every email serves one of the two habits that predict retention. It uses only the five allowed triggers, with skip rules and a day-8 branch that pushes each user to whichever habit they're missing, which goes straight at the 8% to 67% gap.
mistake: Email 5 sets a day-14 goal but compares it to a week-one 8% baseline. The holdout gets no onboarding email at all, so the series is never measured against the old series.
to10: Use one measurement window for the 8% baseline and goal. Add a second holdout on the old series so the win is measured against what we run today, not against silence.

strength: The welcome, recurring-task, platform-branched device email and calm check-in are all very good. The drop list ties the projects email to the persona's 'perfect on Sunday, gone by Wednesday' trap.
mistake: It spends the fifth email on a Pro upsell instead of finishing the habit work, so users who have one habit are never pushed to the second, the step worth 67% retention.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a day-8 'missing habit' email. Move Pro past day 30. Check that set-time reminders really are Pro-only before promising it.

strength: It correctly shifts capacity away from decaying blog traffic and into comparison pages, with clear capacity control, projections, and a practical week-one workflow.
mistake: It puts /vs-google-analytics first and pushes the cookie-banner and cookie-free analytics cheap wins too far down, despite those being high-impression near-page-one queries in Maya's own words.
to10: Move the first week to the cookie-banner rewrite, the cookie-free page retitle, and the Fathom comparison brief, then add a small consolidation plan for decaying blog posts.

strength: It grounds the plan in the right trial economics, showing trials per 1,000 clicks and ranking work by likely trial impact rather than traffic.
mistake: The first week still starts with /vs-google-analytics instead of the cookie-banner and cookie-free analytics wins, and Month 3 includes some unspecified pages that need tighter evidence.
to10: Make week one match the highest-leverage cheap wins, give exact titles/briefs for those pages, and replace the placeholder Month 3 comparison choices with a firm rule tied to Search Console impressions.

strength: It picks recruiting for the right reason, shows the seat math, then builds the page around Priya’s real pain, round robin, routing, and the under-used security page.
mistake: A few copy points assume product specifics like video links, PTO handling, and supported tool logos that should be verified before launch.
to10: Tighten the copy slightly under the 1,000-word limit and verify every product-capability claim against the live product before pasting.

strength: It correctly identifies recruiting as the segment, uses the right math, and frames the A/B test around pain versus round robin outcome.
mistake: It leaves placeholders and homework for the owner, and includes unsupported claims such as three or four emails per interview, text reminders, and bracketed proof slots.
to10: Remove all placeholders, keep claims only to supplied facts or clearly verified product capabilities, and make the CTAs consistent with the brand rules for team buyers.

strength: It puts the forecast miss, margin drop, Customer A churn, runway, and AI-builder economics in the first screen with the right math.
mistake: It is a little less investor-ready because the assumptions block and a few lines read like internal notes rather than a finished email to send.
to10: Tighten the copy, remove or fold in the assumptions, and make the 48-hour pause impact and VP Sales ask sharper.

strength: It leads with the three numbers and bad news, explains the AI-builder margin problem plainly, and ends with specific asks with dates and forwardable copy.
mistake: It assumes a ship date and that the VP Sales role is now New York-based, which should be confirmed before sending.
to10: Confirm the two assumptions and slightly soften the unproven claim that most of the compute rise came from AI-builder projects.

strength: It follows the pilot signal tightly: Controllers/Heads of Finance at 50–300 person SaaS companies with a recent pricing-page change, no links, and an honest 6.8%–7.9% reply expectation.
mistake: The 9-to-4-day proof appears in step 1, when the stronger play would be to keep step 1 entirely about their pricing change and spreadsheet pain, then use proof in a later touch.
to10: Move the proof to step 2 or 4, sharpen step 1 around the pricing-change trigger only, and make the reply ask slightly softer than 'reply yes'.

strength: It correctly identifies the winning segment, the pricing-page trigger, the no-link rule, and gives practical list exclusions and projections from the pilot.
mistake: The invented send window between the 12th and 15th works against the key timing signal, which is to send soon after the weekly pricing-change flag while the change is fresh.
to10: Remove the calendar-window rule and bolder generic watch-list test, keep the sequence tied to fresh pricing-change flags, and soften the meeting-heavy CTAs into lower-friction finance-to-finance replies.

strength: It acts on the two big signals: the Asia-Pacific coverage gap and the fact that writing predicts success far more than years or tools.
mistake: The application is not fully ready to run because it does not include the actual customer-reply prompt, and the piece likely runs over the 1,100-word limit.
to10: Add a ready-to-paste customer email exercise and trim the operational detail while keeping the strong scorecard and APAC-hours positioning.

strength: It is publishable, plain-spoken, honest about salary, hours and weekends, and puts the written customer reply at the center of the process.
mistake: The application reply prompt gives too few facts to test problem-solving well, and the extra 'why this job' question is a weaker signal than the exercise.
to10: Give the written exercise enough customer/account facts to score problem solving as well as tone, and remove or de-emphasize the low-signal motivation question.

strength: It turns the brief’s numbers into the right strategic diagnosis: agency losses are the Semrush fight, while Lite limits and generic multi-site onboarding are self-inflicted leaks.
mistake: The fifth move overlaps with the first and third, so the reporting bet is split into multiple initiatives instead of one sharper plan.
to10: Merge the duplicate reporting moves and make the Lite limits/top-up test the explicit first action this month, since it is the fastest churn win.

strength: It is very clear on where Ahrefs does and does not lose to Semrush, with the key math shown and the PPC parity trap avoided.
mistake: The fifth move, link-data content, is weaker and more generic than the other moves, with less direct connection to the competitive leak or this month’s execution.
to10: Replace the content move with a more direct AWT agency/reporting conversion test or a tighter Lite pricing/limits rollout plan, and make the first-step metrics more specific.

strength: It catches the two big launch risks: creator/author channels drive retained users, and hotkey/settings migration must be a hard launch gate.
mistake: It leaves too many placeholders in the launch copy and has a contradictory channel table, ranking extension authors above X while showing fewer retained users.
to10: Remove the placeholders, add owners to the timeline, tighten the retained-user ranking logic, and make the support/engineering plan fit the stated team without hand-waving.

strength: It is strongly built on the actual signals: community and creators first, migration risk before the code freeze, clear gates, support targets, and usable launch copy.
mistake: It labels the channel table as ranked by users kept while placing extension authors above channels with more absolute retained users, so the ranking rationale should be made explicit.
to10: Clarify the channel ranking as retained-quality plus scale, separate Product Hunt from launch-day attention, and add a slightly richer X thread with author credits in the main post.

strength: It catches the three important signals: Essentials 8+ churn, under-used yearly billing, and the fact that grandfathering means near-term gains must come from retention rather than repricing the base.
mistake: The extra 'bolder move' at the end makes the recommendation feel less like one clear decision and more like a second pricing idea.
to10: Remove the extra future pricing idea, tighten the Agency test math into a simple before/after cohort model, and make the yearly-billing change part of the same test plan.
